one_liner: Rust-built Python video reader over libavcodec for ML loading; its own table beats OpenCV VideoCapture and decord.
what_it_does: A Python extension (PyO3, pip package video-reader-rs) that opens a file path or in-memory bytes and returns uint8 numpy frames. decode() returns one (N, H, W, 3) array for a frame range with optional even temporal subsampling (compression_factor) and resize; decode_gray() returns (N, H, W); decode_fast() returns a Python list of per-frame arrays; get_batch(indices), indexing, slicing and iteration cover random access. The get_batch/len/slicing surface is modelled on decord's VideoReader, but the class (PyVideoReader), constructor options and coverage differ, so it is not a drop-in for decord or for cv2.VideoCapture.
how_it_is_fast: Decoding itself is FFmpeg's libavcodec through ffmpeg-next 9.0.0 with frame-level threading and an automatic thread count, so the gains are pipeline gains. With compression_factor below 1 every packet is still decoded, but only the selected frames go through the FFmpeg filter graph (format=yuv420p, scale with fast_bilinear by default) and the YUV420-to-RGB24 conversion, which uses the SIMD yuv crate (awxkee's yuvutils-rs) instead of swscale. decode() writes into one preallocated ndarray; decode_fast() hands each frame's conversion to tokio tasks on a multi-thread runtime so conversion overlaps decoding, and the GIL has been released during decode since v0.4.2. get_batch picks keyframe seeking or a sequential pass from a cost estimate (GOP size, codec, number of seeks).
when_to_use: Python ML data loading that needs a whole clip or uniformly subsampled frames as RGB uint8 numpy arrays, especially where decord runs out of memory because it allocates for the whole video at open.
High-resolution sources where YUV-to-RGB conversion is a large share of the time; decode_fast() spreads it over cores (6.2 s vs 9.3 s for decode() at full frame rate in the README table).
Training inputs downscaled at read time: resize_shorter_side, resize_longer_side or target_width/target_height run in the FFmpeg filter before conversion, so conversion touches fewer pixels.
Pipelines that already hold encoded video in memory (object storage, queues): v0.4.5 reads bytes, bytearray or BytesIO without a temp file.
Projects that want prebuilt wheels: manylinux_2_34 x86-64/aarch64/riscv64, macOS 14 arm64 and 15 x86-64, Windows amd64, abi3 for CPython >= 3.9, plus PyPy 3.11 and free-threaded 3.14.
when_not_to_use: Sparse random access into long videos: users who measured it found parity or a loss against decord (issue #94: one frame per second from a 2-hour HD video, decord 1:45 vs video_reader 1:55; issue #97 on a Ryzen 5 5600X under Windows 10: decord 12% faster on one 1080p file, video_reader 23% faster on two others). The constructor also demuxes every packet to build its frame and keyframe index.

Workloads that need pixel-identical output to OpenCV or decord: conversion uses its own matrix and range choices (issue #51 reports arrays that differ from cv2), and the BT.2020 and filtered-range colour bugs in issue #152 were fixed on main on 2026-09-28, after the 0.4.5 wheel of 2026-09-25.
10-bit, 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 sources where precision matters: the default and required filter path forces 8-bit yuv420p before RGB24.

GPU-resident tensors or audio: the CUDA path downloads NV12 frames to host and returns numpy (DLPack support is an open PR, #150), non-CUDA hardware acceleration needs a hand-written filter, and there is no audio reader (issue #49 open).

Odd output sizes: from code reading, copy_image sizes the YUV420 buffer as width*(height+height/2), so an odd width or height without a custom filter (native odd dimensions, or a resize that rounds to an odd value) fails with an InvalidData error; choose even resize targets.

integration.form: module (Python extension built from a Rust cdylib with maturin; PyPI wheels; not published as a Rust library crate)
integration.dependencies: numpy; FFmpeg libraries (bundled in the wheels; source builds need FFmpeg development libraries, libclang, pkg-config and maturin, plus the ffmpeg_5 feature for FFmpeg <= 5); Rust crates ffmpeg-next 9.0.0, yuv 0.8.13, ndarray 0.16, tokio 1.48, pyo3 0.27
integration.platforms: Linux (glibc 2.34+) x86-64, aarch64, riscv64; macOS 14 arm64 and 15 x86-64; Windows amd64; CUDA decode only from a source build against a CUDA-enabled FFmpeg
integration.thread_safety: Each PyVideoReader guards its reader with a Mutex, so concurrent calls on one object serialize; decode and get_batch release the GIL (v0.4.2, issue #111), so separate readers in separate threads run in parallel. The FFmpeg log level set by the constructor is process-global.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — decord-like get_batch, len, indexing and slicing, but a different class, constructor and a subset of decord's API; no cv2.VideoCapture-style read/grab interface

gotchas: decode() preallocates the whole (N, H, W, 3) result: the README's full 2004-frame 1472x1472 decode is 13.0 GB (derived from page data), so chunk with start_frame/end_frame. Frame count is the demuxed packet count, and from code reading decode() returns the full preallocated array even if fewer frames come out, leaving trailing all-zero frames.

decode_gray() decodes full RGB first and then applies luma weights 0.2125/0.7154/0.0721 in Rust: it is slower than RGB decode (6.6 s vs 4.2 s in the README table) and its values differ from OpenCV's BT.601 cvtColor gray and from the Y plane.

When the stream has no colour-space tag the matrix is guessed from height (below 720 BT.601, above 1080 BT.2020, otherwise BT.709), so untagged high-resolution video such as the 1472-line benchmark clip is converted with BT.2020.

Custom filter strings must start with format=yuv420p and cannot be combined with resize options or target sizes (a filter containing 'scale' counts as a resize); decode_fast() returns a list, not a stacked array.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The closest sibling is Nelux, whose own numbers are against FFmpeg CLI pipes and torchcodec on Windows with NVDEC; pick video_reader-rs for numpy output, decord-style get_batch with a frame-accurate sequential fallback, and wheels across Linux, macOS, Windows, aarch64 and riscv64. Decoder entries such as dav1d, edge264 or rivet-h26x speed up decoding itself and are complementary, since video_reader-rs uses whatever libavcodec decoder its FFmpeg build provides.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table, decoding one 2004-frame 1472x1472 video to RGB uint8 on an i7-9750H laptop with 15 GB RAM under Ubuntu 22.04: decode_fast 6.2 s vs OpenCV VideoCapture 65 s and decord 18 s at full frame rate, and 3.8 s vs 7.16 s and 14.03 s at compression factor 0.25. FFmpeg, OpenCV and decord versions, the codec and the timing script are not published, decord ran on a different, larger machine, and the OpenCV and decord columns come from a single July 2024 run while the video_reader columns were re-measured at later commits.
status_note: Active (v0.4.5 on PyPI 2026-09-25, last commit 2026-09-30) and MIT for the Rust source, with (L)GPL FFmpeg binaries inside the wheels; frame-accuracy and colour fixes keep landing (decode near GOP boundaries #78, get_batch frames #90 fixed in v0.4.0, colours #153 after the last release), so pin a version and spot-check frames against a reference.
measurement_notes: Measurement flaws behind the catalogued numbers (no correctness bug affects the timings themselves): (1) Mixed-date columns: README history shows the OpenCV and decord numbers unchanged since the first table (7.16 s, 14.03 s, 6.49 s, 20.24 s, 33.96 s), while video_reader cells were replaced at later commits (f 0.25: 6.73 s to 4.2 s; f 0.25 grayscale: 14.11 s to 11.3 s to 6.6 s; f 0.5: 26.76 s, slower than decord's 14.6 s, to 5.5 s), so the current ratios compare 2024 baselines with newer code. (2) Memory pressure: full-rate output is 13.0 GB and f 0.5 output 6.5 GB on a 15 GB laptop (derived from page data); OpenCV's time drops 4.7x from f 0.5 (33.96 s) to f 0.25 (7.16 s) for half the frames, which points to swapping rather than decode speed in the f 1.0 and f 0.5 OpenCV cells (inference). (3) decode_fast returns a Python list of frames rather than one stacked (N, H, W, 3) array, so its column skips the contiguous output the other columns produce. (4) In video_reader the grayscale row is a full RGB decode followed by an RGB-to-gray pass (code read); the OpenCV and decord scripts are not published, but all three columns are slower in gray than in RGB, consistent with the same post-conversion (inference), so the row does not measure a luma-only decode. (5) The independent python-decoders-benchmarks harness (NevermindNilas) lists Video-Reader-RS, but every recorded CI run in history/720p_history.json from 2026-04-26 to 2026-10-01 fails it with "name 'PyVideoReader' is not defined", so it supplies no independent number; decord runs at 145-212 fps there on 720p. Third-party anecdotes in issues #94 and #97 show parity or a loss against decord for sparse sampling. Tier C stands.
